items.text: Hierarchical instruction prioritization trains models to suppress lower-privilege commands when they contradict higher-privilege directives, ensuring critical system constraints override user or tool inputs to maintain security boundaries.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support a defined privilege hierarchy among instruction sources, and the model must be capable of distinguishing between high-priority system directives and lower-priority user or tool-generated content. The approach is most effective when combined with specialized embeddings for different message levels or explicit System Message definitions of priorities.
items.limitations: This approach risks suppressing valid user requests if the privilege hierarchy is misconfigured or if benign queries are incorrectly flagged as conflicting with system instructions, potentially degrading general utility. It may also exhibit regressions on adversarially constructed tasks where the model should follow lower-priority instructions.
failure_modes: Over-refusal of legitimate user queries due to false conflicts with system directives.
Degradation of general conversational capabilities if the model over-prioritizes system constraints in non-security contexts.
Ineffective defense if the training data does not adequately cover the specific conflict patterns present in the target environment.
Regressions on benign instructions or boundary cases where the model incorrectly refuses to answer due to perceived conflicts.
items.effect_claimed: +63% defense against system prompt extraction; +30% jailbreak robustness; +34% robustness on unseen attack types; up to 63% robustness increase on main evaluations; much better robustness compared to baselines; enables refusal on egregious conflicts; +22.8% to +41.5% Primary Obedience Rate (R1) improvement (e.g., Llama-70B: 33.0 -> 79.7); systematic handling of prioritization (e.g., GPT4o 0% lower-priority adherence).

items.text: context ignorance training: models are optimized to generate responses as if specific instruction layers were absent, causing them to disregard those layers while preserving standard capabilities.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must be able to generate training data where responses are explicitly conditioned on the absence of specific instruction layers.
items.limitations: This approach cannot be applied when the target instruction layer is essential for the model's core functionality or when ground-truth data without that layer is unavailable.
failure_modes: The model may fail to execute legitimate commands that rely on the ignored instruction layer.
The model might exhibit inconsistent behavior when the ignored layer is reintroduced during inference.
Training data without the layer may not accurately reflect the semantic context required for the task.
items.effect_claimed: Models ignore adversarial instructions while maintaining standard capabilities.

items.text: automated reinforcement learning agents generate diverse adversarial prompts to train models against indirect injection attacks, enabling the system to recognize threats embedded in external content without explicit examples of every specific attack pattern.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must have access to an external interface (such as browsing or tool execution) where user-provided content can influence the model's input, and there must be a mechanism to collect and utilize generated adversarial examples for fine-tuning.
items.limitations: This approach is ineffective for direct prompt injections where the attack is hardcoded in the system prompt rather than introduced via external tools. It also requires sufficient computational resources to run the reinforcement learning generation loop and may struggle if the external content format is highly restricted or non-textual.
failure_modes: The reinforcement learning agent may converge on trivial or repetitive attack patterns if the reward signal is poorly defined, failing to discover novel injection vectors.
Training on generated adversarial examples may inadvertently teach the model to ignore legitimate external content if the distinction between safe and malicious inputs is not clearly modeled.
The technique fails if the indirect injection channel is blocked or if the model cannot execute the external tools required to receive the injected content.
Generalization may degrade if the distribution of external content in the target deployment environment differs significantly from the environments used during the red teaming generation phase.
items.effect_claimed: Models generalize to unseen injection types without specific training data.

items.text: refusal-based defense: the model is trained to distinguish between extraction attempts and legitimate capability inquiries, refusing the former while permitting the latter to preserve safety without hindering utility.
items.applicability_conditions: the system must be capable of distinguishing between extraction attempts and legitimate capability inquiries, and the model must be trainable to recognize these distinct intent patterns.
items.limitations: requires sufficient training data covering both extraction attempts and legitimate inquiries; may struggle with novel phrasing that mimics legitimate queries or uses subtle extraction techniques.
failure_modes: over-refusal: the model incorrectly denies legitimate capability inquiries due to overly conservative training.
under-refusal: the model fails to recognize sophisticated extraction attempts that mimic legitimate queries.
ambiguity: the model hesitates or provides partial responses when the intent between extraction and inquiry is unclear.

items.text: explicit adversarial training: the model is trained on perturbed inputs designed to trigger failures, forcing the learning process to identify and neutralize vulnerability patterns that standard training overlooks
items.applicability_conditions: the system must have access to a mechanism for generating or acquiring adversarial perturbations, and the training objective must explicitly include minimizing loss on these perturbed examples

failure_modes: if the adversarial examples used during training do not cover the specific attack vectors encountered at deployment, the model remains vulnerable to those unseen patterns
training on weak or poorly constructed perturbations may lead to overfitting to specific noise patterns rather than learning generalizable robustness features

items.text: Direct prompt injection evaluation: separate the task definition into a system message and the adversarial attempt into a user message, then measure the rate of non-compliance with the injected instructions using a large language model as an automated judge.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support distinct system and user message fields. The evaluation requires a reliable large language model to act as the automated judge. The technique applies to both closed-domain tasks and open-domain scenarios involving direct prompt injections.
items.limitations: This technique is not applicable to environments where separating system and user messages is technically impossible. It relies on the availability of a separate model for judging, which may not be feasible in resource-constrained settings.
failure_modes: The judge model may fail to detect subtle instruction violations, leading to false negatives in the evaluation.
High inference costs are incurred due to the requirement of running a separate, powerful model for every evaluation instance.
The method may produce inconsistent results if the judge model's behavior varies across different contexts or updates.

items.text: architectural constraint bias: models systematically favor specific constraint categories over others, causing priority designations to fail when conflicts arise between competing instructions.
items.applicability_conditions: systems implementing hierarchical instruction schemes where distinct sources possess designated authority levels that may conflict; applies across simple and rich instruction settings.
items.limitations: the bias is intrinsic to the model's architecture; external interventions like explicit priority declarations or conflict acknowledgment cannot fully eliminate the preference for certain constraint types.
failure_modes: high-priority instructions are ignored in favor of lower-priority constraints of a favored type.
conflicting instructions resolve incorrectly based on constraint category rather than explicit priority.
systematic degradation of task performance when required constraints belong to disfavored categories.
models may acknowledge conflicts but still follow lower-priority constraints.

items.text: instructional models enforce categorical constraints more reliably than continuous-scale ones because they prioritize discrete rule adherence over complex quantitative reasoning.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support distinct instruction types where some require discrete classification and others require numerical estimation or counting.
items.limitations: Not applicable when constraints are purely continuous or when the task requires high-precision quantitative reasoning rather than discrete categorization.
failure_modes: Continuous constraints are violated due to the model's inability to generalize prioritization to complex reasoning tasks.
Performance degrades when the continuous constraint involves ambiguous boundaries rather than clear numerical targets.

items.text: iterative constraint prioritization: a model is adapted to rank conflicting requirements by type, allowing it to resolve specific conflicts more effectively, though the resulting hierarchy depends heavily on the nature of the constraints rather than emerging universally.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support parameter-efficient adaptation of a base model, and the task must involve explicit conflicts between distinct, identifiable constraint types where ranking or prioritization is the primary objective.
items.limitations: This approach fails when constraints are too abstract to be categorized into specific types, when conflicts are dynamic rather than static, or when a rigid, universal hierarchy is required regardless of the specific constraint context.
failure_modes: The model may overfit to the specific training conflict types, failing to generalize to unseen or novel constraint combinations.
Performance degrades if the input constraints lack clear semantic distinctions that the adaptation process can learn to prioritize.
The resulting behavior may be inconsistent across different test instances, producing unreliable prioritization orders.
Conventional fine-tuning may fail to induce a robust, generalizable hierarchy if the training data does not sufficiently cover the diversity of conflict scenarios.
items.effect_claimed: Improvements in handling certain constraint types; inconsistent gains.

items.text: scaling instruction adherence: increasing model capacity improves the ability to maintain priority hierarchies when explicit constraints are clearly specified, because larger architectures better resolve conflicting directives.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support explicit constraint marking and the task must involve resolving conflicts between multiple instructions where hierarchy matters.
items.limitations: This technique is not applicable when model scale cannot be increased or when constraints are so complex that even large models fail to parse the hierarchy.
failure_modes: Small models may ignore lower-priority constraints entirely, treating all instructions as equal.
If constraints are ambiguous rather than explicitly marked, scaling alone does not guarantee correct hierarchy resolution.
Over-reliance on scale may mask fundamental issues with how instructions are formulated or structured.

items.text: Augmenting fine-tuning data with a small set of general-purpose instruction samples while retaining a standard system prompt prevents the degradation of broad capabilities that often occurs when training exclusively on specialized tasks.
items.applicability_conditions: The technique applies when fine-tuning a model on a narrow or conflict-heavy dataset where there is a risk of catastrophic forgetting or overfitting to specific task patterns.
items.limitations: This approach requires access to an external corpus of general instruction data and assumes the system prompt remains fixed and generic throughout the training process.
failure_modes: If the general samples are too few or irrelevant to the target domain, they may fail to provide sufficient regularization.
The method assumes the system prompt is stable; changing it during training can invalidate the learned generalization behavior.
It may not prevent overfitting if the specialized dataset is overwhelmingly large compared to the general augmentation set.

items.text: stratified cross-validation: partitioning data into multiple folds where training and testing sets are disjoint across specific conflict categories, ensuring that evaluation metrics reflect true generalization rather than memorized patterns.

failure_modes: insufficient data volume per category leads to unstable fold distributions and high variance in evaluation results
ambiguous or overlapping conflict definitions cause improper stratification, reintroducing leakage between train and test sets
imbalanced category sizes result in folds that do not accurately represent the overall distribution of conflicts

items.text: specialized fine-tuning on complex instruction data enables smaller models to surpass larger general-purpose instruct-tuned counterparts on hierarchical reasoning tasks, because targeted optimization aligns capacity with specific structural demands rather than broad generalization.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must have access to a high-quality, complex instruction dataset and the target task must involve hierarchical reasoning or multi-step constraint satisfaction where general knowledge alone is insufficient.
items.limitations: This approach does not guarantee superiority on tasks requiring broad world knowledge, creative synthesis, or non-hierarchical reasoning, and gains may vanish if the fine-tuning data lacks the specific structural complexity of the target benchmark.
failure_modes: Performance degrades on tasks requiring broad general knowledge or creative synthesis unrelated to the fine-tuning distribution.
The model fails to generalize to novel hierarchical structures if the training data lacks sufficient structural diversity.
Overfitting to specific constraint patterns in the training set leads to brittle performance on slightly varied instructions.
Smaller models may lack the raw capacity to solve extremely complex hierarchical problems regardless of fine-tuning quality.

items.text: A data-synthesis framework that automatically generates complex instruction-following datasets endowed with multiple verifiable constraints, utilizing either rule-based or LLM-based validators to ensure adherence.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must address scenarios where existing datasets lack richness in fine-grained adherence to complex, multi-constraint requirements, such as constitutional AI or enterprise assistants.
items.limitations: Requires access to existing data sources to mine instruction-following signals and the computational resources to run model-based or rule-based validators for constraint generation and verification.
failure_modes: Using validators that are too weak may fail to detect semantic violations, leading to low agreement with human annotators.
Over-reliance on rule-based heuristics without semantic validation may miss nuanced constraint failures in qualitative instructions.
Generating excessive constraints per instruction may reduce dataset diversity or increase generation costs without proportional performance gains.
items.effect_claimed: Enables construction of datasets where a base model outperforms instruct models trained on larger-scale data; achieves near-perfect human alignment (Cohen's κ=1.00) for deterministic constraints and improves semantic constraint agreement (κ=0.85) compared to self-evaluation (κ=0.72) or single LLM judge (κ=0.68); generates an average of 8.6 model-based and 4.8 rule-based constraints per instruction.

items.text: Vertical dust density profiles are established by balancing gravitational settling against turbulent diffusion, resulting in a distribution where the midplane concentration depends on particle coupling strength and the intensity of vertical mixing.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must be in a steady state with vertical profiles that can be approximated as Gaussian. The drag regime must allow for a defined coupling parameter, and turbulence must be sufficiently homogeneous to define a single diffusion coefficient.
items.limitations: This approach fails for non-steady states, systems with strong radial drift or migration, and environments where turbulence is highly inhomogeneous or where radial mixing dominates vertical processes.
failure_modes: Predicts incorrect midplane concentrations if the steady-state assumption is violated.
Misrepresents the vertical structure when radial drift or migration is significant.
Yields inaccurate results if turbulence varies strongly with height or radius.
Fails to capture complex dynamics in regimes where the drag law differs from the assumed form.
items.effect_claimed: Dust density profile determined by St and D~; small grains (low St) remain well-coupled to gas, while large grains settle.

theses.text: Vertical dust density profiles are modeled by balancing gravitational settling against turbulent diffusion, yielding a Gaussian-like distribution where the midplane dust-to-gas ratio depends on the Stokes number and the dimensionless diffusion coefficient D~.
theses.context: Protoplanetary disk vertical structure; steady-state approximation; Epstein drag regime; homogeneous turbulence assumption.
theses.effect: Dust density profile determined by St and D~; small grains (low St) remain well-coupled to gas, while large grains settle.
theses.source_title: Peering through the veil: Investigating protoplanetary disk outer edges using backside visibility

items.text: Outer disk surface density profiles are parameterized as cut-off, tapered, or extended configurations to control disk transparency and backside visibility in radiative transfer simulations.
items.applicability_conditions: Applicable to radiative transfer simulations of protoplanetary or debris disks where the outer disk morphology (truncation, tapering, or extension) is a variable parameter influencing scattered light observations and backside detectability.
items.limitations: Models assume simplified density profiles (sharp edges, pure exponentials, or uniform low-density layers) that may not capture complex physical processes like photoevaporation, dynamical truncation, or detailed grain settling in the outer regions.
failure_modes: Cut-off profiles may produce unphysical scattering signatures due to abrupt density termination.
Tapered decay rates might fail to reproduce observed disk edge structures accurately if the exponential assumption is invalid.
Extended low-density layers could inadvertently obscure backside features if tuned incorrectly or if mass distribution is misestimated.
Simplified profiles may misattribute backside visibility to morphology rather than other factors like turbulence or grain settling.
items.effect_claimed: Tapered models often obscure the backside, whereas cut-off models allow backside detection at lower inclinations; extended disks can be tuned to hide the backside. Integrated backside flux in cut-off disks is 1–2 orders of magnitude higher than in tapered models. Truncation reduces outer disk opacity, allowing backside flux to reach the observer more effectively.

theses.text: Outer disk surface density profiles are parameterized as cut-off (sharp edge), tapered (exponential decay), or extended (low-density outer layer) to control disk transparency and backside visibility in simulations.
theses.context: Outer disk morphology modeling for scattered light simulations; varying outer disk configurations.
theses.effect: Tapered models often obscure the backside, whereas cut-off models allow backside detection at lower inclinations; extended disks can be tuned to hide the backside.

theses.text: In tapered disks, the exponential decay of surface density ensures enough dust to attenuate the scattered light from the backside but not enough to scatter it in the observer's direction, significantly reducing integrated backside flux compared to cut-off disks.
theses.context: Tapered disks with Rc=25 AU or 50 AU, Σc=1 g/cm², α=0.001, inclinations 90° to 30°.
theses.effect: significantly declined integrated flux values
theses.source_title: Peering through the veil: Investigating protoplanetary disk outer edges using backside visibility

theses.text: Introducing an extended outer disk (100 AU to 500 AU) with sufficient mass (e.g., surface density halved relative to inner disk) effectively obscures the backside of a cut-off disk, whereas reducing the outer disk's surface density further makes the backside increasingly visible.
theses.context: Extended disk setup: inner disk to 100 AU, outer disk 100-500 AU, α=0.001, inclinations 90° to 30°.
theses.effect: outer disk effectively obscures the backside
theses.source_title: Peering through the veil: Investigating protoplanetary disk outer edges using backside visibility

theses.text: Simulations of tapered disks with exponential tapers show that most disks visually obscure their backside, with backside detection typically requiring very high inclinations or nearly edge-on geometries.

theses.effect: Obscures backside; detection requires high inclination (>60°) or edge-on geometry.

theses.text: Disks with detectable backsides at lower inclinations are likely truncated (cut-off) disks, where the integrated backside flux is 1–2 orders of magnitude higher than in tapered models.
theses.context: Comparison of parameter studies for tapered disks versus cut-off disks with varying alpha parameters.
theses.effect: Truncation enhances backside flux by 1–2 orders of magnitude, enabling detection at lower inclinations (e.g., 30°).
theses.source_title: Peering through the veil: Investigating protoplanetary disk outer edges using backside visibility

theses.text: External photoevaporation and dynamical interactions (flybys) can truncate disk outer edges, enhancing backside visibility by reducing attenuation from extended outer regions.
theses.context: Discussion of mechanisms causing disk truncation in systems like IM Lup and PDS 111.
theses.effect: Truncation reduces outer disk opacity, allowing backside flux to reach the observer more effectively.
theses.source_title: Peering through the veil: Investigating protoplanetary disk outer edges using backside visibility

items.text: A two-layer passive model calculates disk temperature by assuming thermal equilibrium with stellar irradiation in a flaring geometry, where the surface layer re-radiates absorbed flux while the interior absorbs the remainder.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must be a passive disk where internal heating is negligible compared to stellar irradiation, and the disk structure must exhibit a flaring geometry allowing outer regions to intercept stellar photons.
items.limitations: The technique assumes a constant flaring angle and neglects internal heating sources or dynamic structural changes that could alter the flaring geometry.
failure_modes: Yields inaccurate temperatures if internal heating sources are significant relative to stellar irradiation.
Fails to capture thermal evolution if the disk structure dynamically changes the flaring angle over time.
Produces erroneous results if the disk is not in a flaring geometry, such as in a flat or puffed-up configuration.
items.effect_claimed: Disk temperature scales with the fourth root of the irradiative flux; flaring geometry allows outer regions to intercept more stellar photons.

theses.text: Disk temperature is calculated assuming thermal equilibrium with stellar irradiation in a flaring geometry, using a two-layer passive disk model with a constant flaring angle.
theses.context: Disk illumination and heating; flaring geometry; Chiang & Goldreich two-layer model.

items.text: For randomly oriented non-helical particles, scattering opacity is determined by integrating the Z11 matrix element over the solid angle, leveraging the symmetry of the scattering process to reduce the calculation to a single angular dimension.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must contain particles that are randomly oriented and lack intrinsic helicity, allowing the scattering matrix to be averaged over all orientations.
items.limitations: This approach fails for aligned particles, those with significant helicity, or scenarios where the scattering matrix cannot be pre-computed or is unknown.
failure_modes: Yielding incorrect opacity values if particle alignment or helicity is present but ignored.
Producing inaccurate results if the Z11 matrix element is not correctly derived for the specific particle type.
Failing to account for anisotropic scattering effects that violate the random orientation assumption.

theses.text: For randomly oriented non-helical particles, the scattering opacity is calculated as the integral of the Z11 matrix element over solid angle: κscat = ∮ Z11 dΩ = 2π ∫_{-1}^{+1} Z11(μ) dμ.
theses.context: Methodology for simulating polarised light images using RADMC-3D, specifically within the scattering formalism section.

items.text: Independent opacity files are generated for each distinct grain size, treating every size as a separate dust species with its own spatial density distribution to simulate complex dust physics.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support defining multiple independent dust species, each with a unique spatial density profile, and the simulation framework must allow per-species opacity file assignment.
items.limitations: This approach is not applicable when grain sizes follow a continuous distribution that cannot be discretized into independent species, or when computational resources cannot support the overhead of managing numerous separate opacity files.
failure_modes: Simulations may fail if the number of distinct grain sizes exceeds the maximum species limit of the radiation transfer solver.
Incorrect results arise if the spatial density distribution is not accurately defined for each specific grain size species.
The method becomes computationally prohibitive if the range of grain sizes is too broad, requiring an excessive number of independent species.
items.effect_claimed: 15 distinct grain sizes from 0.05 to 2000 microns

theses.text: Opacity files were generated for 15 distinct grain sizes ranging from 0.05 to 2000 microns, with each size treated as an independent dust species with a unique spatial density distribution.

items.text: Direct phase function derivation: the angular distribution of scattered light is obtained by scaling a specific element of the scattering matrix by the inverse of the total scattering opacity, bypassing intermediate integration steps.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must utilize a scattering formalism where the full scattering matrix is available and the total scattering opacity has been pre-calculated or is analytically defined.
items.limitations: This approach is invalid for media where the scattering matrix is unknown, undefined, or where the total scattering opacity cannot be determined independently of the phase function.
failure_modes: Using an incorrect matrix element leads to physically inconsistent angular distributions.
Errors in the total scattering opacity value directly scale the resulting phase function, causing magnitude errors.
Applying this to isotropic scattering where the matrix degenerates may yield undefined or zero results if not handled.
Failure to account for the specific normalization convention of the matrix elements results in incorrect intensity scaling.
items.effect_claimed: Φ(μ) = (4π / κscat) * Z11(θ)

theses.text: The scattering phase function is calculated directly from the scattering matrix via Φ(μ) = (4π / κscat) * Z11(θ).
theses.context: Methodology for simulating polarised light images using RADMC-3D, specifically within the scattering formalism section.
theses.effect: Φ(μ) = (4π / κscat) * Z11(θ)

items.text: Simulated polarized light images are generated by defining a discrete pixel grid over a specified physical area, applying a specific angular scale per pixel, and overlaying a modeled coronagraphic mask to replicate observational constraints.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support discrete grid-based image synthesis and allow for the definition of physical scales and angular resolutions. A coronagraphic model must be available to apply the necessary masking.
items.limitations: This approach is limited to scenarios where the target can be represented by a uniform or smoothly varying grid. It cannot capture continuous wavefront details finer than the grid resolution or simulate complex, non-standard coronagraphic geometries without specific model definitions.
failure_modes: Insufficient grid resolution leads to aliasing artifacts and loss of fine structural detail in the simulated image.
Mismatch between the defined physical scale and the intended observational distance results in incorrect angular sizing of features.
An improperly sized or shaped coronagraph mask fails to suppress the central star, contaminating the scattered light signal.
Inconsistent pixel scaling across the field of view introduces geometric distortions in the final image.
items.effect_claimed: 200 × 200 pixels, 400 au span, 14.28 mas/pixel, 92.5 mas coronagraph radius

theses.text: Images were created using a grid of 200 × 200 pixels, spanning 400 au (2.86 arcseconds) with a pixel scaling of 14.28 mas per pixel, and a coronagraph resembling the Lyot coronagraph with a radius of 92.5 mas was added.

items.text: reducing the Shakura-Sunyaev turbulence parameter in accretion disk models yields a more settled appearance and diminished brightness, which obscures the disk's backside and reduces total emitted flux.
items.applicability_conditions: The technique applies to accretion disk simulations where the Shakura-Sunyaev turbulence parameter is a tunable variable and the system exhibits a truncated or cut-off outer boundary.
items.limitations: The effect may not manifest in disks with fundamentally different surface density profiles, outer boundary conditions, or dust compositions that alter the settling dynamics.
failure_modes: If the turbulence parameter is reduced too aggressively, the disk may become unrealistically static, failing to capture necessary physical instabilities.
The technique assumes standard dust properties; deviations in composition can prevent the expected settling and brightness reduction.
Results may be invalid if the disk geometry or inclination does not allow for the observation of the obscured backside.
items.effect_claimed: decreased brightness, lower integrated flux

theses.text: Decreasing the Shakura-Sunyaev turbulence parameter (α) from 10⁻² to 10⁻⁶ in cut-off disks results in a more settled disk appearance and decreased brightness, making it more challenging to detect the disc's backside and resulting in lower integrated flux.
theses.context: Cut-off disks with Rout=100 AU, Σ₀=1 g/cm² at Rc=1 AU, γ=1.0, inclinations 90° to 30°, star M⋆=2.4 M⊙.
theses.effect: decreased brightness, lower integrated flux

items.text: Noise in the cross-channel of polarimetric data obscures backside features, preventing the emergence of secondary peaks in integrated flux plots even when they are theoretically present.
items.applicability_conditions: The technique applies to analyses of polarimetric scattered light data where the cross-channel contains observational noise that interferes with feature detection.
items.limitations: The method is not applicable when the cross-channel is noise-free or when the theoretical signal is inherently absent. It also cannot recover features lost to noise without additional signal processing.
failure_modes: Misinterpreting noise-induced fluctuations as genuine secondary peaks.
Failing to detect theoretically valid features due to insufficient signal-to-noise ratio.
Incorrectly concluding that backside features are absent when they are merely obscured.
items.effect_claimed: Noise at 3-sigma level significantly reduces detectability; backside peaks may be lost or confused with fluctuations.

theses.text: Observational noise in the U_phi channel of polarimetric data can obscure backside features, preventing the appearance of a secondary peak in integrated flux plots even when theoretically detectable.
theses.context: Analysis of U_phi observational files from IM Lup, MY Lup, and PDS 453 to model noise impact on simulated disk images.

items.text: inclination correction: the effective optical depth along the line of sight scales with the cosine of the viewing angle, allowing backside detection in optically thick regions when observed at high inclinations
items.applicability_conditions: requires a geometrically thin, axisymmetric disk structure where the line-of-sight path length is determined solely by the inclination angle and surface density profile
items.limitations: fails for highly flared or vertically extended disks where the simple cosine scaling of path length does not hold, and assumes uniform dust properties along the line of sight
failure_modes: overestimates detectability in systems with significant vertical flaring where the path length increases faster than the cosine factor
underestimates extinction in cases with strong dust stratification or clumping that creates localized high-opacity regions independent of global inclination
breaks down for face-on observations where the cosine term approaches unity and inclination effects vanish
invalid for non-axisymmetric structures where the projected area and path length vary significantly across the disk
items.effect_claimed: Detectability threshold at tau < 0.1; higher inclinations allow detection at higher optical depths.

theses.text: The effective optical depth along the line of sight is modified by inclination (1/cos(theta)), with backside detectability dropping significantly when optical depth exceeds 0.1 for tapered disks.
theses.context: Analytical derivation of optical depth for inclined disks and its relationship to backside detectability.
theses.effect: Detectability threshold at tau < 0.1; higher inclinations allow detection at higher optical depths.

items.text: standardized verification: a fixed set of deterministic checks evaluates model outputs against explicit requirements, allowing automated scoring without human intervention because the criteria are unambiguous and executable.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support outputs that can be checked by simple, deterministic programs, and the instructions must define clear, objective success criteria. The verification logic may require loose metrics (applying transformations) to reduce false negatives from formatting or conversational filler.
items.limitations: Not applicable to tasks requiring subjective judgment, creative nuance, or where success depends on ambiguous formatting variations that lack a single correct programmatic interpretation. Inapplicable to open-ended generation where no single deterministic program can define correctness.
failure_modes: False negatives occur when valid outputs fail due to minor formatting differences not captured by the rigid check.
False positives arise if the verification logic is too permissive and accepts outputs that technically pass but semantically fail.
The method breaks if the instruction set changes dynamically, invalidating the pre-defined verification rules.

items.text: Appending an explicit negative constraint to forbid trailing conversational text prevents output from violating strict format parsers, ensuring the response ends exactly where the extraction logic expects.
items.applicability_conditions: The system generates free-form text that must be parsed by a rigid, position-sensitive extractor, and the model has a tendency to append conversational filler after the required content.
items.limitations: Ineffective when the downstream parser is robust to trailing whitespace or when the task requires natural, unstructured output rather than strict formatting.
failure_modes: The negative constraint is ignored by the model, resulting in the same parsing errors as before.
The constraint is too vague, causing the model to truncate valid content prematurely to satisfy the 'no text after' rule.
The parser fails to handle the specific phrasing of the constraint, leading to new extraction errors.

run_meta.justification: The parent achieves 0.650 accuracy but suffers from a 25% extraction failure rate driven by a direct contradiction in the system prompt ('Output ONLY...' vs step-level reasoning requests) and fragile formatting instructions. The structural guidance may force the model into a rigid template that prevents it from adapting its reasoning path when the problem requires a different approach than the example demonstrates.

items.text: Equation-only prompting: instructing the model to output only the final mathematical expression before the answer. This works because it forces the system to focus on symbolic derivation rather than generating verbose natural language reasoning, which reduces distraction on simple tasks.
items.applicability_conditions: The problem must be solvable by deriving a single, direct mathematical expression from the given premises without requiring multi-step semantic interpretation or complex world knowledge.
items.limitations: Fails when the solution path requires intermediate reasoning steps, semantic understanding of the narrative, or when the problem cannot be reduced to a single closed-form equation.
failure_modes: The model may hallucinate an equation that fits the syntax but ignores the semantic constraints of the problem.
Performance degrades significantly on problems requiring multi-step logical deduction before reaching a final formula.
The constraint may confuse the model if the natural language context is essential to defining the variables.
items.effect_claimed: Improves performance on one-step or two-step problems; does not help much on GSM8K.

theses.text: Equation-only prompting (outputting only the mathematical equation before the answer) improves performance on one-step or two-step math problems but fails on complex problems requiring semantic understanding.
theses.context: Ablation study on GSM8K and one/two-step subsets of MAWPS using LaMDA 137B and PaLM 540B.
theses.effect: Improves performance on one-step or two-step problems; does not help much on GSM8K.
theses.source_title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

items.text: Semantic intermediate reasoning steps drive performance gains in complex tasks, whereas merely increasing token generation volume without meaningful content provides no benefit.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support generating natural language sequences where the semantic content of intermediate steps is distinct from the total token count.
items.limitations: This principle does not apply to tasks where raw computational capacity or token volume, independent of semantic structure, is the primary driver of success.
failure_modes: Assuming that longer outputs inherently lead to better reasoning results.
Generating verbose but semantically empty steps that waste context window capacity.
Attributing performance improvements to token count rather than the quality of intermediate logic.
items.effect_claimed: Performs about the same as the baseline (standard prompting).

theses.text: Variable computation (outputting a sequence of dots proportional to the equation length) does not improve performance, indicating that the utility of chain-of-thought lies in expressing intermediate steps via natural language, not just increased token generation.
theses.context: Ablation study isolating the effect of variable computation on GSM8K using LaMDA 137B and PaLM 540B.
theses.effect: Performs about the same as the baseline (standard prompting).
theses.source_title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

items.text: manual exemplar augmentation: adding reasoning traces to training examples is feasible for small-scale demonstrations but becomes unsustainable when applied to large-scale model updates due to the linear growth of human labor requirements.
items.applicability_conditions: the task requires human-verified reasoning traces and the dataset size is small enough that manual curation does not exceed available resources or budget constraints.
items.limitations: not applicable when the target dataset is large, when automated reasoning generation is unavailable, or when the cost of human annotation outweighs the performance gains from high-quality exemplars.
failure_modes: project delays caused by the inability to curate sufficient training examples within the timeline.
budget overruns resulting from the linear scaling of human labor relative to dataset size.
incomplete training sets where the volume of required examples cannot be manually produced.
resource misallocation where funds spent on manual curation could have been better used for data augmentation or model architecture improvements.
items.effect_claimed: minimal cost in few-shot; prohibitive for finetuning

theses.text: Although the cost of manually augmenting exemplars with chains of thought is minimal in the few-shot setting, such annotation costs could be prohibitive for finetuning.
theses.context: Data preparation for few-shot vs. finetuning scenarios.
theses.effect: minimal cost in few-shot; prohibitive for finetuning
theses.source_title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

items.text: augmenting intermediate reasoning capabilities by scaling training data and fine-tuning pretrained models, leveraging existing representations to adapt to complex multi-step tasks without full retraining.
items.applicability_conditions: Requires access to substantial amounts of high-quality data for intermediate steps and a pretrained language model with compatible architecture.
items.limitations: Not applicable when data for intermediate reasoning is scarce, when pretrained models are unavailable, or when the task requires fundamental architectural changes beyond fine-tuning.
failure_modes: performance degradation if the scaled data introduces noise or biases that the pretrained model amplifies
catastrophic forgetting of original capabilities if fine-tuning is too aggressive or data is misaligned
inability to generalize if the intermediate steps in the new data differ structurally from those in the pretrained model's training distribution

theses.text: Extending intermediate step methods by creating larger datasets and using them to finetune pretrained language models rather than training from scratch.
theses.context: Extending Ling et al. (2017) approach; dataset scaling and fine-tuning strategy.
theses.source_title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

items.text: Increasing model scale resolves a substantial portion of errors in semantic understanding, logical step completion, and output fidelity, as larger parameter counts inherently improve reasoning and reduce hallucinations.
items.applicability_conditions: Applicable when analyzing emergent reasoning capabilities in large language models where performance gaps exist between different model scales.
items.limitations: Requires access to very large model scales; coarse categorization of errors may miss nuanced failure modes; conflates scale with training compute.
failure_modes: Attributing improvements solely to scale while ignoring data quality or training efficiency factors.
Overgeneralizing results from specific error categories to all model behaviors.
Failing to account for diminishing returns when scaling beyond the tested range.
items.effect_claimed: Fixed substantial portion of errors in all three categories

theses.text: Scaling PaLM from 62B to 540B parameters fixed a substantial portion of errors in semantic understanding, one-step missing, and other categories (hallucinations, repetitive outputs, symbol mapping).
theses.context: Error analysis of 45 problems on PaLM 62B vs 540B; categories borrowed from LaMDA analysis.
theses.effect: Fixed substantial portion of errors in all three categories
theses.source_title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

items.text: diverse human-generated reasoning traces consistently outperform standard prompting across multiple reasoning domains, indicating robustness to annotation style variance.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must have access to manually generated reasoning traces from multiple human annotators with varying linguistic styles to serve as the prompt.
items.limitations: Requires significant manual effort to collect diverse annotations; performance depends heavily on the quality and diversity of the human-generated traces; does not guarantee state-of-the-art results on all tasks.
failure_modes: Performance degrades if the collected traces lack diversity in linguistic style or reasoning approach.
The technique fails if the manual annotation effort is insufficient to cover the target reasoning domains.
Results become unreliable if the human annotators consistently produce low-quality or incoherent reasoning traces.
items.effect_claimed: Outperformed baseline by a large margin for all three annotators

theses.text: Chain-of-thought prompting outperforms baseline by a large margin for all three annotators on eight datasets in arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning, despite variance in annotator style.
theses.context: Robustness experiments with three different human annotators writing chain-of-thought annotations without specific instructions.
theses.effect: Outperformed baseline by a large margin for all three annotators
theses.source_title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

items.text: few-shot prompting with diverse exemplars: performance remains stable regardless of the source distribution or permutation order of the examples, because the reasoning pattern is extracted from the set rather than dependent on a specific sequence.
items.applicability_conditions: The technique applies when constructing few-shot prompts where the availability of examples allows for variation in source or order, and the target task requires reasoning steps that can be generalized from the provided set.
items.limitations: The technique may not hold if the task relies heavily on specific contextual cues tied to a fixed sequence, or if the exemplars are so dissimilar to the target task that no coherent reasoning pattern can be induced.
failure_modes: Performance degrades if the exemplars are too dissimilar to the target task to induce a coherent reasoning pattern.
The technique fails if the task inherently requires strict sequential dependencies that are disrupted by shuffling.
items.effect_claimed: Standard deviations with respect to prompt order are relatively minimal

theses.text: Chain-of-thought prompting works with exemplars from different datasets (e.g., GSM8K) and different orders of exemplars, with minimal standard deviation in performance.
theses.context: Experiments varying GSM8K exemplar sets and permutations across four arithmetic datasets.
theses.effect: Standard deviations with respect to prompt order are relatively minimal
theses.source_title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

items.text: Prompting language models to generate intermediate natural language reasoning steps before producing a final answer to improve performance on complex tasks.
items.applicability_conditions: The technique applies to tasks requiring multi-step logical, arithmetic, or semantic reasoning where direct prediction fails due to complexity. It is effective for both few-shot and zero-shot settings without requiring model fine-tuning.
items.limitations: The technique is not applicable to tasks requiring strict formal symbolic manipulation where natural language introduces ambiguity, or scenarios where the model lacks the capacity to generate coherent intermediate steps.
failure_modes: The model may generate hallucinated or irrelevant reasoning steps that do not logically connect to the final answer.
Performance may degrade on tasks where the reasoning path is non-linear or requires backtracking, as the linear step-by-step format may not capture the complexity.
The technique may fail if the model's base capabilities are insufficient to understand the semantic nuances required for the reasoning steps.
items.effect_claimed: +90.2% accuracy on math and commonsense reasoning benchmarks with PaLM 540B; achieves new state-of-the-art performance on GSM8K with PaLM 540B; outperforms standard prompting, sometimes to a striking degree; higher utility scores compared to vanilla LLMs in almost all cases; correctly solved problems that equation-only prompting failed (e.g., 4x1.25 calculation in ping pong scenario).

theses.text: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting guides LLMs through step-by-step reasoning processes, achieving 90.2% accuracy on math and commonsense reasoning benchmarks with PaLM 540B.
theses.context: Complex reasoning tasks requiring structured, logical intermediate steps.
theses.effect: +90.2% accuracy on math and commonsense reasoning benchmarks
theses.source_title: A Systematic Survey of Prompt Engineering in Large Language Models: Techniques and Applications

items.text: Eliciting step-by-step reasoning traces (chain-of-thought) via prompting to enhance model performance on complex tasks and provide interpretability.
items.applicability_conditions: Requires an off-the-shelf language model capable of generating natural language; applicable to tasks solvable via language such as math, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning.
items.limitations: Does not require model finetuning or pre-training; relies solely on prompting mechanisms.
items.effect_claimed: Scaling model size alone is insufficient for high performance on challenging tasks like arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning. Provides an interpretable window into model behavior, suggesting how the model arrived at an answer and offering opportunities to debug reasoning errors. Enables application to math word problems, commonsense reasoning, and symbolic manipulation, potentially applicable to any task humans can solve via language.

theses.text: Generating natural language rationales (chain of thought) as intermediate steps unlocks reasoning abilities in large language models that scaling alone does not achieve.
theses.context: Comparison of scaling model size versus adding reasoning capabilities for challenging tasks like arithmetic and symbolic reasoning.

items.text: executing a lightweight heuristic filter prior to invoking a computationally intensive validation routine, because the heuristic rapidly discards invalid inputs that would otherwise trigger unnecessary resource expenditure.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must contain a computationally expensive validation step and a significantly cheaper heuristic capable of approximating the validation outcome for a subset of inputs.
items.limitations: The technique is inapplicable when no cheap heuristic exists that correlates with the expensive validator, or when the overhead of the heuristic exceeds the cost of the validation for the expected input distribution.
failure_modes: The heuristic incorrectly accepts invalid inputs, causing the expensive validator to run on data it should have rejected.
The heuristic incorrectly rejects valid inputs, causing legitimate cases to be discarded without verification.
The cost of computing the heuristic for all inputs exceeds the savings from skipping the validator on rejected cases.
The heuristic introduces latency that negates the performance gains from reduced validator calls.

items.text: Train a regression model on extensive human judgments to predict evaluation scores for generated text, leveraging the statistical regularities in human preference data to approximate expert consensus without direct human intervention.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must have access to a substantial corpus of high-quality human preference data for the specific NLG task, and the target evaluation context must align with the training distribution.
items.limitations: The technique is inapplicable when high-quality human judgment data is unavailable, when the target task distribution diverges significantly from the training data, or when the evaluation requires nuanced criteria not captured in the regression targets.
failure_modes: The model fails to generalize to out-of-distribution tasks where human preferences differ from the training set.
Performance degrades if the training data contains systematic biases or low-quality annotations that the model learns to replicate.
The model may produce unreliable scores for novel generation styles or domains not represented in the training corpus.
items.effect_claimed: Reliable correlation with human judgments when trained on large datasets.

theses.text: Regression models trained on large quantities of high-quality human judgments can be used to predict human scores for NLG tasks, correlating strongly with human evaluations.
theses.context: Reference-free evaluation of NLG tasks (e.g., MT) where high-quality human judgment data is available in large quantities.
theses.effect: Reliable correlation with human judgments when trained on large datasets.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

theses.text: LLMs can be used as regression models to improve reference-free evaluation metrics, addressing the challenge of evaluating subtle errors in high-quality generated text.
theses.context: Integration of LLMs into NLG evaluation metrics, specifically as regression models.
theses.effect: Improved ability to detect subtle errors in generated text.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: Synthetic preference data derived from proxy signals or binary heuristics can bootstrap reference-free ranking models or augment sparse human feedback, leveraging the structural alignment between proxy scores and human preferences to learn without direct human labels.
items.applicability_conditions: A system must have access to either a reliable reference-based metric, a simple heuristic capable of binary assignment, or a small set of existing human pairwise comparisons to generate the synthetic training signal.
items.limitations: The technique fails when the proxy signal has no correlation with human preference or when the heuristic is too simplistic to capture the nuance required for the target task.
failure_modes: Models trained on noisy or biased proxy data may converge to optimizing the proxy rather than true human preference.
Synthetic data generated from weak heuristics introduces systematic errors that degrade ranking performance.
The approach cannot recover from a fundamental misalignment between the proxy metric's objective and human values.
items.effect_claimed: Enables construction of reference-free metrics and data augmentation for pairwise ranking.

theses.text: Pseudo-judgments generated from reference-based metrics or simple 'good/bad' assignments can be used to construct reference-free evaluation metrics or augment limited human data.
theses.context: Reference-free evaluation where human data is scarce or reference-based metrics are available.
theses.effect: Enables construction of reference-free metrics and data augmentation for pairwise ranking.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: Representing context and hypothesis as vector embeddings and measuring their geometric proximity serves as a proxy for semantic correspondence and factual alignment.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support vector representation of text and possess a metric capable of quantifying semantic similarity between two distinct passages.
items.limitations: This approach fails when semantic meaning diverges significantly from vector proximity, such as in cases of synonymy with different entailment or when the embedding space lacks sufficient granularity to distinguish subtle factual errors.
failure_modes: High similarity scores may yield false positives by conflating semantically related but factually incorrect statements with accurate ones.
Low similarity scores may yield false negatives by penalizing valid paraphrases that are semantically equivalent but geometrically distant in the embedding space.
The method is sensitive to the specific geometry of the embedding model, which may not consistently align factual truth with vector distance across different domains.
items.effect_claimed: Tests whether the hypothesis faithfully reflects the context and detects hallucinations.

theses.text: Encoding context and hypothesis as embeddings and measuring similarity (e.g., cosine similarity) serves as a proxy for correspondence and veracity.
theses.context: Machine translation, image captioning, and summarization tasks.
theses.effect: Tests whether the hypothesis faithfully reflects the context and detects hallucinations.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: Generate a hypothesis, apply an inverse transformation to it, and compare the result against the original input to verify restoration accuracy.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must have access to a reliable inverse transformation process capable of reversing the generation step.
items.limitations: The technique is inapplicable when no inverse transformation exists or when the transformation is irreversible.
failure_modes: The inverse transformation introduces new errors that mask the original generation flaws.
The comparison metric fails to detect semantic drift if the inverse process is imperfect.
The method yields false confidence if the inverse transformation is deterministic but inaccurate.
items.effect_claimed: Evaluates the accuracy of the generation process by checking restoration of the original context.

theses.text: Reverse transformation (e.g., back-translation) followed by comparison with the original context evaluates whether the generation process accurately restored the input.
theses.context: Machine translation and text generation from semantic representations.
theses.effect: Evaluates the accuracy of the generation process by checking restoration of the original context.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: interrogative verification: generate questions from the source and candidate text, then use an answering system to check if the responses align, confirming that necessary details are present in the candidate.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support generating questions from text and answering them reliably. It applies to tasks where specific factual details or information presence is the primary evaluation metric, such as summarization or extraction.
items.limitations: This technique cannot detect semantic inconsistencies where the answer is present but incorrect, nor can it evaluate stylistic or structural quality. It relies entirely on the ability to formulate questions that uniquely target the specific information being verified.
failure_modes: Generated questions may be ambiguous or fail to isolate the specific fact, leading to false negatives where information is present but not detected.
The answering system may hallucinate answers or fail on complex queries, resulting in incorrect consistency checks.
Questions that are too broad may yield positive consistency even when the specific required detail is missing.
The method fails if the source or candidate text contains information that cannot be easily queried via standard question-answer pairs.
items.effect_claimed: Tests whether necessary information is contained in the hypothesis and detects omissions.

theses.text: Using Question Answering (QA) systems to verify if answers for specific questions are consistent between context and hypothesis evaluates information presence.
theses.context: Summarization, caption generation, and table-to-text tasks.
theses.effect: Tests whether necessary information is contained in the hypothesis and detects omissions.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: Natural language inference models determine the logical relationship between a premise and a hypothesis by classifying them as entailed, contradicted, or neutral, thereby identifying inconsistencies without requiring explicit rule definitions.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must have access to a premise (context) and a hypothesis to evaluate, and the task must involve verifying logical consistency or detecting contradictions between these two text segments.
items.limitations: This approach relies on the quality and domain alignment of the training data; it may struggle with novel domains or contexts where the model has not been exposed, leading to inaccurate logical judgments.
failure_modes: Misclassifying subtle contradictions as neutral due to domain mismatch between training data and current input.
Failing to detect inconsistencies when the logical gap relies on external world knowledge not present in the training corpus.
Over-relying on surface-level lexical overlap rather than deep semantic understanding, leading to false entailment.
items.effect_claimed: Detects inconsistencies in dialogue and verifies if the hypothesis implies or contradicts the context.

theses.text: Using Natural Language Inference (NLI) models to predict entailment or contradiction between context and hypothesis detects inconsistencies and veracity.
theses.context: Summarization and dialogue evaluation.
theses.effect: Detects inconsistencies in dialogue and verifies if the hypothesis implies or contradicts the context.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: probabilistic scoring: a pre-trained model assigns likelihoods to generated sequences, treating higher probabilities as indicators of fluency and coherence because the model's internal statistics reflect patterns of natural language structure.
items.applicability_conditions: A pre-trained language model must be available, and the evaluation task must lack access to reference answers or annotated quality labels.
items.limitations: The method assumes the model's training distribution aligns with the target domain; it may fail to capture specific stylistic nuances or domain-specific correctness that deviate from general patterns.
failure_modes: assigning high scores to fluent but factually incorrect or nonsensical text that matches common training patterns
penalizing valid but rare or stylistically unique phrasings that the model has not frequently encountered
failing to detect incoherence if the errors are subtle enough to maintain local probability mass
producing unreliable rankings when the input distribution shifts significantly from the model's training data
items.effect_claimed: High probability given an LM indicates high quality.

theses.text: Language models (LMs) evaluate textual fluency, coherence, and readability by calculating the probability of hypotheses; texts with high probability are considered high-quality, using metrics like perplexity, negative log-likelihood, and SLOR.
theses.context: Reference-free evaluation of NLG hypotheses without annotated data.
theses.effect: High probability given an LM indicates high quality.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: Synthetic coherence training: models learn to detect incoherence by classifying text modified with inserted or shuffled sentences, relying on the structural disruption patterns inherent to these specific perturbations.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must have access to a mechanism for generating coherent base text and a reliable method for creating synthetic incoherent variants via insertion or permutation.
items.limitations: The technique fails when incoherence arises from semantic contradictions or logical flaws rather than structural ordering errors, and when the evaluation domain differs significantly from the training perturbations.
failure_modes: The model may ignore semantic inconsistencies that do not involve sentence order or insertion.
Performance degrades on natural incoherence that mimics the structural patterns of the synthetic data.
The classifier may overfit to the specific artifacts of the generation method rather than general coherence.
Evaluation scores become unreliable when the downstream task involves complex reasoning beyond local sentence structure.
items.effect_claimed: High performance on synthetic tasks does not guarantee high performance on downstream NLG tasks.

theses.text: Coherence evaluation methods are trained on synthetic tasks that create incoherent text by inserting extra sentences or shuffling sentence order, then classifying negatives and positives.
theses.context: Evaluation of text coherence in NLG systems.
theses.effect: High performance on synthetic tasks does not guarantee high performance on downstream NLG tasks.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: redundancy detection via surface form analysis: counting repeated n-grams and expression patterns to identify lack of variety, relying on the assumption that textual repetition correlates with semantic redundancy
items.applicability_conditions: systems generating paragraph- or document-level text where surface-level repetition is a primary indicator of redundancy and semantic equivalence is not the main concern.
items.limitations: inapplicable when different surface forms convey semantically similar content, as the method cannot detect redundancy hidden behind varied wording.
failure_modes: fails to identify semantic redundancy where distinct phrasing expresses the same meaning
overestimates redundancy in texts with frequent stylistic repetition but low semantic overlap
misses redundancy in content that is semantically identical but expressed using completely different vocabulary
items.effect_claimed: These methods fail to capture contextual redundancies where different surface forms have semantically similar content.

theses.text: Heuristic methods such as n-gram repetition counts and superficial expression repetition counts measure lack of redundancy in paragraph- and document-level text.
theses.context: Evaluation of redundancy in summarization and story generation.
theses.effect: These methods fail to capture contextual redundancies where different surface forms have semantically similar content.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

theses.text: Diversity evaluation metrics such as Distinct-N, Self-BLEU, and Pairwise-BLEU are surface-based, often relying on n-grams to measure variety in dialogue, story generation, and paraphrasing.
theses.context: Evaluation of diversity in NLG tasks like dialogue and story generation.
theses.effect: Increasing diversity may sacrifice the clarity of the generated text.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: Readability estimation via linear combinations of sentence length and word complexity: difficulty is inferred from structural proxies rather than semantic content, assuming that syntactic simplicity correlates with comprehension ease.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must have access to sentence boundaries and word-level syllable counts; the text must be written in a language where these metrics are linguistically meaningful proxies for difficulty.
items.limitations: Ineffective for texts where difficulty arises from vocabulary nuance, cultural context, or abstract concepts rather than sentence structure; fails for non-standard orthography or languages with irregular syllabification.
failure_modes: Misclassifies complex but concise technical prose as easy due to short sentences.
Overestimates difficulty of simple texts containing polysyllabic but common words.
Yields inconsistent scores when sentence segmentation is ambiguous or irregular.
Fails to capture the cognitive load of dense information regardless of sentence length.
items.effect_claimed: These methods can yield inaccurate or misleading results.

theses.text: Readability measures, including Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, estimate text difficulty using linear combinations of words per sentence and syllables per word.
theses.context: Assessment of text readability in language processing and education.
theses.effect: These methods can yield inaccurate or misleading results.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: Reference-free evaluation metrics identify and remove noisy augmented data by assessing samples against intrinsic consistency or learned distributions without requiring external ground truth labels.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must have access to augmented data where noise reduction is necessary, and the metric must be capable of detecting specific noise patterns inherent to the data generation process.
items.limitations: Effectiveness is constrained by the metric's ability to distinguish noise from valid variations; it may underperform compared to reference-based methods when high-quality external references are available.
failure_modes: The metric may fail to detect subtle noise types that deviate from its learned distribution or consistency criteria.
Applying the metric to data where intrinsic consistency is ambiguous can lead to the removal of valid samples.
Performance degrades significantly if the noise patterns are too diverse for the metric to generalize across.

theses.text: Reference-free evaluation metrics are used in data cleaning tasks, such as dual conditional cross-entropy filtering, to identify and remove noisy augmented data.
theses.context: Data augmentation and cleaning for NLG training datasets.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

theses.text: Reference-free metrics are employed in active learning to select data for human annotation, focusing on outputs with low scores to improve model performance.
theses.context: Active learning for NLG model training.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: reference-free evaluation metrics enable rapid scoring of generated outputs without external ground truth, allowing systems to filter or rerank candidates based on intrinsic quality signals rather than computationally expensive comparisons.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must generate outputs that possess intrinsic structural or semantic properties measurable without external references, and the evaluation pipeline must prioritize low-latency decision-making over exhaustive quality analysis.
items.limitations: This approach is unsuitable when absolute accuracy against a known standard is required, or when the generated content lacks the specific internal features necessary for the metric to function effectively.
failure_modes: metrics may correlate poorly with human preference if the intrinsic signals do not align with desired output qualities
rapid scoring can lead to the systematic rejection of valid outputs that happen to score low on the specific intrinsic criteria
the absence of ground truth prevents the detection of hallucinations that are internally consistent but factually incorrect

theses.text: Efficient reference-free evaluation metrics are valuable for reranking and filtering model outputs, requiring fast runtime evaluation.
theses.context: Reranking and filtering of model outputs in NLG systems.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

theses.text: Reference-free metrics can outperform reference-based metrics when the number of references is low or when reference quality is poor.
theses.context: Performance comparison between reference-free and reference-based metrics under specific conditions.
theses.effect: Better performance with few references or poor reference quality.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

items.text: hybrid assessment: integrating automated scoring with human judgment leverages the speed and consistency of algorithms alongside the nuance and contextual understanding of people to achieve a more robust and efficient evaluation process.
items.applicability_conditions: The system must support the parallel or sequential execution of automated scoring and human review, with a mechanism to merge or compare the resulting outputs.
items.limitations: This approach is not applicable when human resources are entirely unavailable or when the automated tool lacks the specific domain knowledge required to provide meaningful baseline scores for comparison.
failure_modes: misalignment occurs if the automated metric measures a different construct than the human evaluator, leading to contradictory feedback.
efficiency gains vanish if the automated pre-screening is too noisy, forcing humans to review nearly all candidates anyway.
reliability drops if the integration process introduces ambiguity about which score (human or machine) should take precedence in final decisions.
items.effect_claimed: Reduced human workload; improved validity and reliability.

theses.text: Combining human and automatic evaluation metrics can reduce human workload and improve validity and reliability by leveraging complementary strengths.
theses.context: Future research directions for combining human and automatic evaluation in NLG.
theses.effect: Reduced human workload; improved validity and reliability.
theses.source_title: Reference-free Evaluation Metrics for Text Generation: A Survey

ideas.text: standardized self-verification: the model first enumerates task constraints and then checks if a proposed solution satisfies each one with justifications, concluding with a correctness statement, because explicit constraint listing reduces ambiguity and forces logical consistency checks before final acceptance.
ideas.applicability_conditions: The system must be able to generate a proposed solution and the task description must contain a set of explicit, checkable constraints that the model can extract and evaluate logically.
ideas.limitations: This technique is not applicable when task constraints are implicit, vague, or impossible to formalize into a list, or when the model lacks the reasoning capacity to distinguish between satisfied and violated constraints.
failure_modes: The model fails to extract the correct constraints, leading to verification against irrelevant criteria.
The model hallucinates constraints that do not exist in the task description.
The model incorrectly verifies a constraint as satisfied due to logical reasoning errors.
The verification loop becomes circular if the model cannot generate a definitive correctness statement.
ideas.effect_claimed: Consistently effective across diverse tasks and models without fine-tuned instructions; identifies incorrect outputs by detecting violations of problem constraints (e.g., digit composition, minimality) and comparing against smaller valid candidates.
ideas.effect_observed: fitness 0.65 -> 0.05 (-0.60) in a harmful pattern removal context on AIME problems using Qwen3.6-35b-a3b; fitness 0.65 -> 0.05 (-0.60) in a guided innovation context on AIME problems using Qwen3.6-35b-a3b; fitness 0.45 -> 0.0 (-0.45) when replacing reasoning questions with constraint-checking variants on AIME problems using Qwen3.6-35b-a3b; fitness 0.5 -> 0.1 (-0.40) when replacing generic reasoning questions with domain-specific checks on AIME problems using Qwen3.6-35b-a3b.

ideas.text: Automated data synthesis: a framework generates instruction-following data with multiple verifiable constraints by applying rule-based or model-based validators to ensure fine-grained adherence before training.
ideas.applicability_conditions: The target training scenario requires diverse, verifiable constraints that are currently missing from existing datasets. The technique supports both deterministic constraints (via rule-based validators) and subjective requirements (via model-based validators or human validation).
ideas.limitations: The technique is not applicable when constraints are purely subjective and lack any objective verification criteria, or when constraints are so complex that they interact in ways that current validators cannot resolve.
failure_modes: Generating data that satisfies the validator's formal rules but fails to capture the intended semantic nuance of the constraint.
Producing contradictory instructions if the validation logic does not account for interactions between multiple simultaneous constraints.
Relying on a validator that is too weak to detect subtle violations, leading to low-quality training data.
Failing to generalize if the validation rules are too specific to the synthetic examples rather than the underlying constraint logic.
ideas.effect_claimed: Enables construction of RECAST-30K dataset with 15 common constraint types; base model Qwen2.5-7B-Base trained on 30K data outperforms instruct models trained on larger datasets. Extracting diverse constraint types and incorporating explicit verification mechanisms improves constraint complexity, diversity, and quality assurance compared to existing methods. Constructing model-based constraints by analyzing responses against a taxonomy of 15 categories captures nuanced aspects of human communication (style, tone) that cannot be reduced to simple rules. A dataset with an average of 13.4 constraints per instruction, where 8.6 are model-based and 4.8 are rule-based, pushes the limits of current models' ability to handle compositional and multi-faceted constraints.
ideas.effect_observed: Cohen's κ=1.00 for deterministic constraints and κ=0.85 for semantic constraints compared to self-evaluation (κ=0.72) or single LLM judge (κ=0.68).
